title: BIS confirms fintechs beat banks on cross-border cost, AML gaps follow
summary: BIS research crowns non-bank fintechs as the cheapest cross-border payment channel, but cheaper rails bring thinner compliance controls. Plus: the HKMA STR quality overdue obligation that 25% of authorised institutions still haven't closed.
script:
ALEX: The BIS dropped research this week confirming what practitioners have suspected for a while. Non-bank fintechs like Wise and Remitly are now materially cheaper than correspondent banking channels for retail cross-border transfers, and they are beating stablecoins on cost too. Jordan, my read is that this is less a payments story and more a supervisory-priority story.

JORDAN: I agree the payments angle is almost secondary at this point. But I want to push back slightly on where you land the supervisory emphasis. Because when I read BIS research like this, my Monday morning question is not what will regulators do. It is what my risk appetite statement says about these rails and whether it still reflects reality.

ALEX: Say more on that.

JORDAN: Well, the BIS confirmation that fintechs are winning on cost means volume is following them. More volume on lighter-touch rails means the aggregate financial crime exposure on those corridors is growing, even if the individual transaction values stay small. And a lot of AML programmes in traditional banks still treat fintech-to-bank correspondent flows as lower risk by default, because the counterparty is a regulated firm. That assumption is getting harder to defend.

ALEX: That is a fair challenge. Where I land differently is on the stablecoin comparison. The BIS research positions stablecoins as more expensive than fintechs right now, which I think gives supervisors a temporary argument to focus attention on the fintech rails rather than crypto. But that window is not long. Solana's Alpenglow upgrade went live this week. The developers describe it as the most significant architectural change to the protocol since its 2020 mainnet launch. Revised consensus, faster block propagation, materially different transaction finality times. If stablecoin settlement on Solana becomes genuinely faster and cheaper, the cost comparison in that BIS data shifts.

JORDAN: Right, and the compliance infrastructure does not move at the same speed as a protocol upgrade. That is the gap that concerns me. A Virtual Asset Service Provider, a VASP, building on Solana today has to reassess its transaction monitoring calibration when finality times change. The rules of what constitutes a completed transaction for suspicious transaction report, STR, purposes potentially shift too.

ALEX: Although I want to be careful not to overstate the Alpenglow risk on day one. Validator support for a separate XRP Ledger bug fix actually failed to hit the eighty percent supermajority threshold this week, which is a reminder that protocol upgrades in crypto rarely land cleanly or on schedule. So the Solana change is live, but how it behaves in practice over the next weeks matters more than the launch announcement.

JORDAN: Fair. Though I would say to any VASP compliance officer listening: do not wait for the operational evidence to accumulate before you brief your technology team. The question to ask now is whether your Know Your Transaction infrastructure tracks finality state, not just transaction broadcast. Those are different things on Solana post-Alpenglow.

ALEX: So what should practitioners do on the BIS cross-border finding specifically?

JORDAN: First, if you are at a bank that receives settlement flows from fintech PSPs, look at how those counterparties are classified in your correspondent risk framework. If they sit in a lower-risk bucket simply because they are regulated in a FATF-compliant jurisdiction, that classification needs stress-testing. The BIS research is essentially confirming that volume on these rails is growing fast, and volume growth without a corresponding review of your monitoring thresholds is a classic gap finding. Second, for anyone running a tranche-two readiness programme in Australia, this is directly relevant. Section 84 of the AML/CTF Act requires your annual programme review to reflect your current risk environment. If your risk environment now includes materially higher fintech corridor volumes, your Part A assessment needs to say so.

ALEX: Let us turn to the obligations desk, because there are two items I want to make sure do not slip past. The first is the HKMA AML and CFT Guideline, specifically paragraph 11, which governs the annual self-assessment return. For authorised institutions in Hong Kong, that return covers customer due diligence, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, STR filing, training, governance, and independent audit. The submission deadline was September the thirtieth.

JORDAN: If you have not submitted, that is overdue and it is a conversation you need to have with your HKMA relationship manager today, not next week.

ALEX: And then there is the still-actionable overdue item that I think deserves more than a passing mention. The HKMA issued a thematic review of STR narrative quality in the fourth quarter of last year, and deficiency letters went to approximately twenty-five percent of the authorised institution population in early 2026. Closure of those findings is outstanding.

JORDAN: Twenty-five percent is not a tail event. That is a systemic issue with how the industry is writing suspicious transaction reports. And in my experience, STR narrative quality is one of those things that sounds like a documentation problem but is actually a governance problem. If your narratives are thin, it usually means the investigation workflow is thin. Analysts are closing cases without enough interrogation of the underlying activity.

ALEX: I would push back slightly on the characterisation that it is always governance. Sometimes it is resource. You have skilled investigators writing five or six STRs a day under time pressure, and the narrative quality degrades simply because there is not enough time to write well.

JORDAN: That is real, but that is still a governance problem. It is a resourcing decision that someone senior made. The HKMA is not going to distinguish between the two when they review the narrative and find it inadequate.

ALEX: Fair point. So what does closure of that thematic finding actually look like in practice?

JORDAN: You need three things in place. A reviewed and updated STR narrative template that reflects the HKMA's specific feedback from the deficiency letter. An evidenced training intervention for the investigators and the supervisors reviewing their work. And a quality assurance sampling process that can demonstrate, on paper, that narrative standards have improved since the letter was received. If you are the MLRO at an authorised institution and those three things are not documented, that is your action before the end of next week.

ALEX: The December year-end is also bringing up the periodic CDD review obligation under Section 16 of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, the AMLO, for high-risk customers. Minimum annual, risk rating reaffirmed or adjusted, STR considered if the pattern has materially changed. That deadline is ten weeks away.

JORDAN: Ten weeks sounds comfortable until you count the number of high-risk customers in your book and the average time your team takes to complete a full periodic review. Do that calculation today and compare it against available capacity in November. If the numbers do not stack up, escalate now while there is still time to bring in resource.

ALEX: And the Bitcoin ETF inflow number, one point zero eight billion dollars across three trading sessions, we should mention it briefly. The institutional appetite signal is real, but from a supervisory lens what it tells me is that the regulated crypto investment product channel is deepening. FATF Recommendation 15 obligations for VASPs and financial institutions dealing in crypto assets are not going to get lighter in that environment.

JORDAN: Agreed, and worth flagging for any compliance team at a licensed fund administrator or custodian with crypto ETF exposure: your transaction monitoring scope should explicitly cover ETF creation and redemption flows, not just secondary market trading. Those are different risk profiles.

ALEX: Before we close, the thing to watch over the next two weeks is how APAC regulators respond to the BIS cross-border research. It is the kind of third-party validation that gives supervisors cover to sharpen their fintech corridor expectations, and it will likely surface in examiner conversations before it surfaces in formal guidance.

JORDAN: If any of what we covered today, particularly the STR quality obligation, felt uncomfortably close to home, that is exactly the point. The full source links and obligation register are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. Back here Monday.
